chapter: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property (Theft)
title: Theft
official_summary: Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, commits theft.
ingredients: The property taken must be movable property
It must be taken out of the possession of another person
The taking must be without that person's consent
There must be dishonest intention to take the property
The property must be moved in order to accomplish the taking
punishment: Imprisonment of either description for a term up to 3 years, or fine, or both. For a first conviction where the value of the stolen property is under ₹5,000 and it is returned or restored, the court may impose community service instead. For a second or subsequent conviction, rigorous imprisonment of not less than 1 year, extendable to 5 years, and fine.
classification_note: Reflects the general BNSS First Schedule pattern for this offence; the exact bail position can be affected by value of property and prior convictions — confirm against the official Schedule for a specific case.
exclusions: If entry into a house or building was involved, see house-trespass/house-breaking (Section 331) and theft-in-dwelling aggravations
If force, fear of instant hurt, or violence was used, see Robbery (Section 309)
aggravating_factors: Theft committed in a dwelling house, or in a building/tent/vessel used as human dwelling or property custody, may attract enhanced punishment under related provisions
Repeat offence increases minimum sentence
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property (Robbery and Dacoity)
title: Robbery
official_summary: Theft is robbery if, in committing the theft or in carrying away the stolen property, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, hurt, or wrongful restraint. Extortion is robbery if committed in the presence of the victim by putting them in fear of instant death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, inducing them to deliver the property there and then.
ingredients: There is an underlying act of theft or extortion
Force, or the threat of instant death/hurt/wrongful restraint, is used
The threat or force is directed at the victim or someone present with them
For theft-based robbery: death, hurt, or wrongful restraint is caused or attempted while committing the theft or carrying away property
For extortion-based robbery: the fear of instant harm is used to induce the victim to hand over property in that moment
punishment: Rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine; if the robbery is committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise, imprisonment may extend to 14 years. Attempt to commit robbery: imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. If hurt is voluntarily caused during the robbery: imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine.
triable_by: Magistrate of the First Class (Court of Session where committed on a highway between sunset and sunrise, or where hurt was caused)
classification_note: Confirm the exact triable court for the specific aggravation involved against the official BNSS First Schedule.
exclusions: If five or more people jointly commit the robbery, see Dacoity (Section 310)
If there was no force or threat of instant harm, see Theft (Section 303)
aggravating_factors: Use of a deadly weapon
Committed at night on a highway
Hurt voluntarily caused to the victim
Multiple offenders acting together
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XIX — Of Criminal Intimidation, Insult, Annoyance
title: Criminal Intimidation
official_summary: Whoever threatens another person with any injury to their person, reputation, or property (or to someone they are interested in), intending to cause alarm, or to make them do something they are not legally bound to do, or omit something they are legally entitled to do, as a means of avoiding the threat, commits criminal intimidation.
ingredients: A threat of injury to person, reputation, or property
The threat is directed at the victim or someone the victim cares about
Intention to cause alarm to the person threatened
OR intention to compel an act/omission as the price of avoiding the threat
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or fine, or both.
classification_note: This entry covers the general (non-aggravated) form. See the related entry for threats of death or grievous hurt, which carry enhanced punishment.
exclusions: If the threat specifically involves death, grievous hurt, destruction by fire, or an offence punishable with death/life imprisonment, see the aggravated provision under Section 351(3)
aggravating_factors: Threat made anonymously or with a concealed identity attracts an additional term up to 2 years
special_law_warning: If the threat was made online (SMS, WhatsApp, social media, email), cyber-crime provisions under the Information Technology Act, 2000 may also be relevant.
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XIX — Of Criminal Intimidation, Insult, Annoyance
title: Criminal Intimidation — Threat of Death or Grievous Hurt (Aggravated)
official_summary: Where the threat referred to in Section 351(1) is to cause death or grievous hurt, or to destroy property by fire, or to impute unchastity to a woman, or is a threat of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment or with imprisonment for a term up to 7 years, the offence attracts enhanced punishment.
ingredients: All the ingredients of general criminal intimidation
The specific content of the threat is death, grievous hurt, destruction of property by fire, imputation of unchastity, or an offence carrying a serious sentence
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 7 years, or fine, or both.
classification_note: Some references list this aggravated form as cognizable in certain circumstances; verify against the official BNSS First Schedule for the exact classification applicable to the specific threat alleged.
aliases: criminal intimidation with threat of death
hinglish_aliases: jaan se maarne ki dhamki di
context_terms: threatened with a weapon and to kill
exclusions: If no specific threat of death/grievous hurt/fire was made, see the general provision, Section 351(1)-(2)
aggravating_factors: Threat made anonymously or with concealed identity
Threat accompanied by display of a weapon
special_law_warning: If the threat was made online, cyber-crime provisions under the Information Technology Act, 2000 may also be relevant.
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XVIII — Of Offences Relating to Documents and Property Marks
title: Forgery
official_summary: Whoever makes a false document or electronic record, or part of one, with intent to cause damage or injury to the public or any person, or to support a claim, or to cause a party to a contract to enter it, or with intent to commit fraud, commits forgery.
ingredients: Making, or altering, a document or electronic record so that it becomes false
Doing so with the intention to cause damage or injury to the public or a person
OR to support a claim/title, or to cause someone to part with property, or to enter a contract
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or fine, or both.
classification_note: This entry covers basic forgery. See the related entry for forgery intended for the purpose of cheating, which carries enhanced punishment.
exclusions: If the forged document was specifically created to cheat someone, see the aggravated provision under Section 336(3)
aggravating_factors: Forgery of a valuable security, will, or authority to make/transfer a valuable security attracts a separate, higher punishment under related provisions
Forgery intended to harm reputation
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XVIII — Of Offences Relating to Documents and Property Marks
title: Forgery for the Purpose of Cheating
official_summary: Where a false document or electronic record is forged with the intention that it shall be used for the purpose of cheating, the offence attracts enhanced punishment compared with basic forgery.
ingredients: All ingredients of forgery under Section 336(1)
Specific intent that the forged document be used to cheat someone
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 7 years, and fine.
classification_note: Confirm classification against the official BNSS First Schedule for this specific aggravated form.
context_terms: fake documents used to get a loan
forged papers used to claim money
used a forged document to deceive
aggravating_factors: Document used to obtain money or property from a bank or institution
Repeated use of the forged document against multiple victims
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property (Cheating)
title: Cheating
official_summary: Whoever, by deceiving a person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces that person to deliver property, or to consent to the retention of property, or to do or omit to do something which they would not have done or omitted if not deceived, and which causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation, or property, commits cheating.
ingredients: Deception of the victim by the accused
Fraudulent or dishonest inducement as a result of that deception
The victim delivers property, or consents to its retention, or does/omits an act
Damage or harm (or likelihood of it) to body, mind, reputation, or property results
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 3 years, or fine, or both.
classification_note: This entry covers general/basic cheating. See the related entry for cheating that induces delivery of property or a valuable security, which carries enhanced punishment.
exclusions: If the cheating specifically induced delivery of property, money, or a valuable security, see the enhanced provision under Section 318(4)
aggravating_factors: Victim was someone the accused was bound to protect their interests (e.g. a fiduciary relationship)
special_law_warning: If the fraud was carried out online, over the phone, or through digital payment systems, provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000 relating to cybercrime may also be relevant.
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property (Cheating)
title: Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property
official_summary: Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property, or to make, alter, or destroy any valuable security (or anything signed/sealed that could become a valuable security), attracts enhanced punishment.
ingredients: All ingredients of cheating under Section 318(1)
The deception dishonestly induces delivery of property, or the making/altering/destruction of a valuable security or a document capable of being converted into one
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 7 years, and fine.
classification_note: Confirm classification against the official BNSS First Schedule; treatment can vary with the value of property involved.
hinglish_aliases: online paise ka fraud kiya aur paisa le liya
aggravating_factors: Large sum of money or high-value property involved
Victim is elderly or otherwise vulnerable
Offence committed as part of an organised scam
special_law_warning: If the fraud was carried out online, over the phone, or through digital payment systems, provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000 relating to cybercrime, and RBI/banking-fraud reporting channels, may also be relevant.
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body (Of Offences Affecting Life)
title: Murder
official_summary: Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. Where a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on grounds such as race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, or personal belief, each member of the group is punished with death or imprisonment for life, and fine.
ingredients: An act causing death

Done with the intention of causing death, or with intention to cause bodily injury known to be likely to cause death, or with knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death

The act does not fall within any of the statutory exceptions (e.g. grave and sudden provocation, exceeding the right of private defence) that reduce the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder
punishment: Death, or imprisonment for life, and fine. Enhanced/mandatory treatment applies where five or more persons acting in concert commit murder on specified discriminatory grounds.
context_terms: died as a result of the attack
exclusions: If death did not occur but there was intent/act capable of causing death, see Attempt to Murder (Section 109)

If the killing falls within a recognised exception (grave and sudden provocation, private defence exceeded, etc.), it may instead be culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 105) — a fact-specific determination for investigators and courts
aggravating_factors: Group of five or more acting on discriminatory grounds
Use of a deadly weapon
Premeditation
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body (Of Attempts)
title: Attempt to Murder
official_summary: Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge, and under such circumstances that, if death were caused, the act would amount to murder, and by such act causes hurt to any person, or the act is otherwise capable of causing death, shall be punished — even though death does not result.
ingredients: An act done with the intention or knowledge that, if it caused death, would amount to murder
The act need not actually cause death
If hurt is caused in the course of the act, the punishment is more severe
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 10 years, and fine; if hurt is caused to any person by such act, imprisonment for life or the punishment above. Where the offender is already under sentence of imprisonment for life and causes hurt, punishment may extend to death or imprisonment for life (meaning the remainder of natural life).
context_terms: attacked with a knife and victim survived
exclusions: If death actually resulted, see Murder (Section 103)
If there was no intention/knowledge capable of amounting to murder, see the relevant Hurt/Grievous Hurt provisions instead
aggravating_factors: Use of a deadly weapon
Hurt caused during the attempt
Offender already serving a life sentence
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body (Of Hurt)
title: Voluntarily Causing Hurt
official_summary: Whoever causes bodily pain, disease, or infirmity to any person, intending to cause hurt, or knowing it to be likely that such hurt would be caused, is said to voluntarily cause hurt.
ingredients: Bodily pain, disease, or infirmity is caused to the victim
The act is done with the intention of causing hurt, or with knowledge that hurt is likely to result
punishment: Imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both.
exclusions: If the injury meets the statutory definition of grievous hurt (e.g. fracture, permanent disfigurement, danger to life), see Grievous Hurt (Section 117)
If a deadly weapon or dangerous means was used, related aggravated hurt provisions may apply instead
aggravating_factors: Use of a weapon or dangerous means, even without grievous injury, may attract a related aggravated provision
Multiple assailants acting together — see also Rioting, Section 191
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body (Of Hurt)
title: Voluntarily Causing Grievous Hurt
official_summary: Whoever voluntarily causes hurt, where the hurt intended or known to be likely, and the hurt actually caused, amounts to grievous hurt (as defined — e.g. emasculation, permanent loss of sight/hearing, loss of a limb, permanent disfigurement of the face/head, fracture or dislocation of a bone, or any hurt which endangers life or causes severe bodily pain / inability to follow ordinary pursuits for 15 days or more), commits this offence.
ingredients: Hurt is caused to the victim
The hurt caused falls within the statutory definition of 'grievous hurt'
The offender intended, or knew it likely, that grievous hurt (of some kind) would result
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 7 years, and fine. Where the grievous hurt causes permanent disability or the victim is reduced to a persistent vegetative state, rigorous imprisonment of not less than 10 years, extendable to imprisonment for life (meaning the remainder of natural life).
classification_note: Where the offence causes permanent disability, classification and the appropriate trial court can differ — confirm against the official BNSS First Schedule.
context_terms: hit with an iron rod causing fracture
exclusions: If death resulted, see Murder (Section 103) or Attempt to Murder (Section 109) depending on the facts
If injuries are minor and do not meet the grievous-hurt threshold, see Voluntarily Causing Hurt (Section 115)
aggravating_factors: Use of a deadly weapon such as a knife or firearm
Permanent disability or vegetative state caused
Offence committed by five or more persons on discriminatory grounds
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property (Of House-Trespass and House-Breaking)
title: House-Trespass and House-Breaking (Punishment)
official_summary: Punishes lurking house-trespass and house-breaking — unlawfully entering or remaining in a building used as a human dwelling (or for custody of property), including entry by concealment, scaling, breaking open a lock, or similar means listed in the definition section. Punishment increases where the entry occurs at night, or is committed in order to commit an offence, especially theft.
ingredients: Entry into, or unlawful remaining within, a building used as a human dwelling or for custody of property
The entry/exit is by one of the specified unlawful means (e.g. concealment, scaling a wall, forcing a lock, using a false key)
For the aggravated forms: the trespass/break-in occurs between sunset and sunrise, or is committed in order to commit an offence such as theft
punishment: Basic house-trespass/house-breaking: imprisonment up to 2 years, and fine. Committed at night: imprisonment up to 3 years, and fine. House-breaking to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment: up to 3 years (up to 10 years if the intended offence is theft). Committed at night for such a purpose: up to 5 years (up to 14 years if the intended offence is theft).
classification_note: The aggravated night house-breaking-to-commit-theft form may be non-bailable in some references — confirm the specific sub-clause against the official BNSS First Schedule.
context_terms: entered my house and stole jewellery
exclusions: If nothing was taken and no trespass-related entry occurred, this section does not apply
The actual taking of property inside the house is separately theft (Section 303); this section addresses the unlawful entry itself
aggravating_factors: Entry at night
Entry to commit theft specifically
Use of force or tools to break in
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter VII — Of Offences Relating to Kidnapping, Abduction
title: Kidnapping
official_summary: Kidnapping takes two forms: (a) conveying a person beyond the limits of India without their consent (or that of someone lawfully entitled to consent on their behalf); or (b) taking or enticing a child, or a person of unsound mind, out of the keeping of their lawful guardian, without the guardian's consent.
ingredients: For kidnapping from India: conveying a person beyond India's limits without valid consent
For kidnapping from lawful guardianship: taking or enticing a minor or a person of unsound mind out of the keeping of their lawful guardian, without the guardian's consent
A good-faith claim to guardianship (e.g. by a parent believing themselves entitled to custody), made without unlawful or immoral purpose, is excepted
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 7 years, and fine.
context_terms: took a child without the parents' consent
enticed a minor away from home
took person out of India without consent
exclusions: If the kidnapping was carried out with intent to murder, extract ransom, or subject the victim to grievous hurt or slavery, see the aggravated provision under Section 140
aggravating_factors: Ransom demanded
Intent to murder or cause grievous hurt
Victim subjected to confinement or exploitation
special_law_warning: Where the victim is a child, provisions of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, or other child-protection laws may also be relevant depending on the facts.
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter VII — Of Offences Relating to Kidnapping, Abduction
title: Kidnapping or Abducting in Order to Murder, for Ransom, or to Subject to Grievous Hurt/Slavery
official_summary: Aggravated forms of kidnapping/abduction: (1) where done with intent to cause the victim's murder, or to place them in a situation where they are likely to be killed; (2) where accompanied by threats of death or hurt, or by demand for ransom, in order to compel the government, any person, or any foreign state/organisation to act or abstain from acting; (3) where done to secretly and wrongfully confine the victim; (4) where done to subject the victim to grievous hurt, slavery, or unnatural acts.
ingredients: An underlying act of kidnapping or abduction

One of the specified aggravating intentions or circumstances: intent to murder, ransom demand with threats, secret wrongful confinement, or intent to subject the victim to grievous hurt/slavery/unnatural acts
punishment: Kidnapping/abduction with intent to murder: imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine. Kidnapping for ransom with threats of death/hurt: death, imprisonment for life, and fine. Kidnapping for secret and wrongful confinement: imprisonment up to 7 years, and fine. Kidnapping to subject to grievous hurt, slavery, or unnatural acts: imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine.
exclusions: If none of the aggravating intentions (murder, ransom, confinement, grievous hurt/slavery) is present, see the general kidnapping provision, Section 137
aggravating_factors: Ransom actually collected
Victim harmed while in captivity
Organised/gang involvement
special_law_warning: Where the victim is a child, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 and the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 may also be relevant depending on the facts.
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property (Mischief)
title: Mischief (Damage to Property)
official_summary: Whoever, with intent to cause wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, or knowing that they are likely to cause wrongful loss or damage, causes destruction of property, or a change in it, or in its situation, diminishing its value or utility, or affecting it injuriously, commits mischief.
ingredients: Destruction of property, or a change to it or its situation
The change diminishes the property's value or utility, or affects it injuriously
Intention to cause wrongful loss/damage, or knowledge that such loss/damage is likely
The property need not belong to the person causing the loss; loss to any person suffices
punishment: Basic mischief: imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine, or both. Where loss/damage is actually caused: imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine, or both. Where the loss caused is ₹20,000 or more but less than ₹1,00,000: imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both. Where the loss caused is ₹1,00,000 or more: imprisonment up to 5 years, or fine, or both. Mischief committed after making preparation for causing death or hurt in order to commit it or facilitate escape: imprisonment up to 5 years, and fine.
triable_by: Any Magistrate (Magistrate of the First Class for the higher-value tiers)
classification_note: Cognizability and bail position for the higher-value tiers may differ from the base offence — confirm the applicable tier against the official BNSS First Schedule.
exclusions: If the damage was accidental with no intent or knowledge of likely loss, mischief does not apply
If the property was taken away rather than merely damaged, see Theft (Section 303)
aggravating_factors: High monetary value of loss
Mischief committed to facilitate another offence or an escape
Preparation made for causing death or hurt in connection with the mischief
special_law_warning: Damage to a motor vehicle may also engage insurance-claim and Motor Vehicles Act procedures.
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023

chapter: Chapter XI — Of Offences Against the Public Tranquillity
title: Rioting
official_summary: Whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member of it, in pursuit of the assembly's common object, every member of that assembly is guilty of rioting.
ingredients: There is an unlawful assembly (five or more persons sharing a common unlawful object)
Force or violence is used by the assembly, or by any of its members
The force/violence is used in prosecution of the assembly's common object
Every member sharing that common object is liable, not only the person who directly used force
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or fine, or both. Where the rioter is armed with a deadly weapon, or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death: imprisonment of either description up to 5 years, or fine, or both.
triable_by: Any Magistrate (Magistrate of the First Class where armed with a deadly weapon)
context_terms: gang of people beat him up
exclusions: If fewer than five persons were involved and there was no common unlawful object, rioting does not apply — see instead the relevant Hurt/Grievous Hurt provisions for the individual assailants
aggravating_factors: Members armed with deadly weapons
Serious injury caused during the rioting — see also Grievous Hurt, Section 117
Rioting connected with an unlawful assembly formed for a further unlawful purpose
source: India Code — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Act No. 45 of 2023
